Kulwinder: Yes. I suppose I did. They're good curtains.
Kirsty: I bet they're really neat.
Kulwinder: The hems are perfect. Nobody notices but me.
Kirsty: I'm like that with drawing. I'll rub out one line about fifty times. Nobody else would know it was wrong.
Kulwinder: You draw? What do you—

Gemma: Hiya! Hello, I'm Gemma.
Neil: Neil. Hello.
Gemma: Hi Neil. Where are you calling from?
Neil: Halifax.
Gemma: Oh, nice. I'm Taunton, down in Somerset. What do you do, then?
Neil: Stonemason. Restoration, mostly. Churches, chapels, old mills.
Gemma: Oh wow, that's not one you hear every day. Like carving and that?
Neil: Some carving, when I'm lucky. A lot of it's repair. Taking out stone that's failed and putting new in, and repointing. Last week I was taking out someone else's cement pointing on a chapel in Hebden Bridge. Somebody'd done the whole gable in hard cement maybe thirty year ago, and it traps the water in, so the stone does the breaking instead of the mortar. Faces just come off in sheets. It should've been lime. It's always lime on a building that age. Folk think cement's stronger, so it must be better, and it's not. It's vandalism, frankly.
Gemma: Vandalism! Strong words.
Neil: It's true, though.
Gemma: No, I believe you. It's like when people put the wrong dressing on a wound because it looks sturdier, and it just keeps all the gunk in. I'm a nurse, sorry, that's the only thing I've got to compare it to.
Neil: Nah, that's fair, actually. Same principle. It's got to breathe.
Gemma: It's got to breathe. There you go. We're basically in the same trade.
Neil: I wouldn't go that far.
Gemma: Ha, fair. Erm, so what do you do when you're not doing stone?
Neil: Walk. Swim, outdoors. I was in Gaddings Dam on Sunday.
Gemma: Outside? In this weather?
Neil: It's not that bad once you're in. The first minute's awful. After that you stop thinking about owt else.
Gemma: That's the bit I'd never get past, the first minute. I do parkrun, that's my limit. Vivary Park on a Saturday. I'm not fast, I'm just sort of there.
Neil: That's most of it. Turning up.
Gemma: Do you watch any sport? Liam, my partner, has got me into the rugby.
Neil: Rugby league. Halifax Panthers.
Gemma: Oh, is that different? We watch Bath sometimes, and the Six Nations.
Neil: That's union. Different game.
Gemma: Is it very different? Sorry, I genuinely don't know.
Neil: Thirteen players, not fifteen. Fewer stoppages. Er, less standing about in heaps. I'm biased.
Gemma: Less standing about in heaps, that's a selling point. I'll tell Liam, he'll be livid. I mostly go for the pub after anyway, to be honest.
Neil: Can't argue with that bit.
Gemma: Did you always want to do stone, then? Like, from school?
Neil: Er. Not exactly. I was good at art. Teacher wanted me to go to art college. I did an apprenticeship instead, because it paid. I sometimes think about it.
Gemma: About the art college?
Neil: Yeah. Then I carve a bit of tracery for a church window and I think, well, this is drawing, just slower.
Gemma: That's actually really lovely, drawing, just slower. Do you still sketch, then, like on—

Katarzyna (goes by Kasia): Erm, I don't remember the names. There was a big painting with a boy being asked questions by soldiers, everybody standing around him. I stood there a long time.

Neil: Hello.

Kirsty: Burnley.

Kirsty: Is it hard, carving?
Neil: It's slow. You can't put stone back once it's off. So you think a lot before you hit it. Er, I like that, though. You can't rush it, and nobody can make you.
Kirsty: That sounds nice, actually. Nobody rushing you.
Neil: It is, mostly. Till a project manager turns up.
Kirsty: Do you find old things in them? The buildings?
Neil: Sometimes. Found a mason's mark last month on a mill in Sowerby Bridge. Little arrow with a cross on it, cut into the bed of a stone. Whoever put it there reckoned nobody'd ever see it. I'd say seventeen-hundreds, from the tooling.
Kirsty: Oh, that's lovely. It's like a signature, isn't it? Somebody's just saying, I was here. I think about that with the mill chimneys round me. Kirsty: My dad used to take me past them. He knew which mill was which. He's not here now, so.

Kirsty: Do you draw them, mills?

Kirsty: I'd like that. I'd have to look up the buses.

Kirsty: Erm, did you want to do art, then? Like properly?
Neil: Teacher wanted me to go to art college. I didn't. Went for the apprenticeship.
Kirsty: I started a BTEC. Didn't finish it.
Neil: Doesn't stop you drawing.
Kirsty: No. I suppose not.
Neil: You can tell from that lock you look properly. That's the bit they can't teach you anyway.
Kirsty: Oh. Erm. Thank you. I don't know what to say to that.
Neil: Don't have to say owt.
Kirsty: Is that us, then?

Nicola: Hello! Oh, hiya, you must be Kulwinder.
Kulwinder: Yes. Hello.

Kulwinder: Hayes. You?
Nicola: Lancaster. Erm, do you work, or...?

Kulwinder: Workroom did my back. Bent over a machine twenty years.
Nicola: Have they got you on a physio sheet as well? I do mine every single morning.

Nicola: Same! Before the kettle, otherwise I talk myself out of it.
Kulwinder: Mm. So you're arty, then. The prints on your wall.

Kulwinder: It's not mine, to be honest. Galleries. I don't get it. Someone puts a chair in a room and people stand round it.

Kulwinder: That's different. A hem has a job.

Kulwinder: Is the wool good? Moth?
Nicola: No moth. Lovely heavy wool, nineteen-seventies, I think.
Kulwinder: Then yes. You don't patch it, you replace the whole lining. If you patch it, it pulls, and it'll go again by the shoulder. People always patch. Then it looks cheap and you can't sell it for what it's worth. A proper lining, that coat is maybe sixty, seventy pounds.

Kulwinder: You're in Lancaster.
Nicola: There's a post office!
Kulwinder: Ha. Haan, maybe. We'll see.
Nicola: I mean it, you know. People pay a fortune for vintage that's been done right.
Kulwinder: Most people don't know what done right is.

Kulwinder: Is that the bell?
